corrected_value.title: The Everyday Belief Bias: Belief in the Claim of a Political Argument Predicts the Perceived Quality of the Argument.

decisions.quote:
Deans-Browne, C., & Singmann, H. (2024). The Everyday
Belief Bias: Belief in the Claim of a Political Argument
Predicts the Perceived Quality of the Argument. PsyArXiv.
https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/x6ehu
decisions.reason: Throughout the paper (Abstract lines 17-20, Introduction lines 52-55 and 83-84, Task section lines 184-185, Discussion lines 568-571), the authors explicitly state that they replicate their Everyday Belief Bias Task from Deans-Browne & Singmann (2024). While the shipped row records metadata for a later 2026 Cognition publication of that study (DOI 10.1016/j.cognition.2025.106257), that title, year, and DOI do not appear anywhere in the primary text. Following the codebook rule to copy the citation and DOI as printed in the supplied text's reference list, blind target 0 is correct and maps to row 2320.

decisions.quote:
We also replicate the belief consistency effect found
previously in the Everyday Belief Bias Task (Deans-Browne
& Singmann, 2024); participants think arguments are of
better quality if the arguments are also in line with their
beliefs. We also replicate that the maximum belief bias effect
was larger than the largest effect of argument type (i.e., the
average difference in argument quality ratings between good
and authority-based arguments). Furthermore, we replicated
the failure to find a linear or quadratic interaction between
argument type and belief consistency, suggesting that the
effect of argument type is somewhat similar irrespective of
how in line the argument is with an individual’s belief.
decisions.reason: The authors explicitly report replicating all tested findings from Deans-Browne & Singmann (2024): good arguments were rated higher than bad (inconsistent and authority-based) arguments, the belief consistency effect was replicated, the maximum belief consistency effect exceeded the largest argument-type effect, and the absence of an argument type by belief consistency interaction was replicated (with the comparison between inconsistent and authority-based bad arguments serving as a new extension).

decisions.quote:
In a
replication of our Everyday Belief Bias Task (Deans-Browne
& Singmann, 2024), we investigate this question using a
paradigm that consists of two parts. In the first part, we
measure participant’s individual beliefs about eight claims
each referring to a political topic (e.g., Abortion should be
legal). In the second part, participants rated an argument for
each of these claims that was deemed as either good,
inconsistent (containing internal inconsistencies), or authoritybased (being centered around appeals to authority).
decisions.reason: The study collected new data from a fresh Prolific sample (N = 152 analyzed) to re-test and extend the findings of the previously published Everyday Belief Bias Task study (Deans-Browne & Singmann, 2024), making it a replication.
